new_statements.quote: The second point of note is that there is no melodic marking of accents. Higher pitch (or even lower pitch, as would appear in a language like Danish) is nowhere used to mark accent. Wolof is nevertheless typologically a language with stress.13 The basic stress-placement rule is as follows: stress falls on the first syllable of lexemes unless the second syllable is long, in which case it falls on the latter (Sauvageot 1965: 41–44; Njie 1982: 53; Ka 1988: 219–242, 1994). [fn. 13] There exists no experimental study of stress realization in Wolof. Perceptibly, its main correlate appears to be vowel quality, in that stressed vowels are more clearly articulated than unstressed vowels.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is on the first syllable of the lexeme by default; if the second syllable contains a long vowel, stress moves to that second syllable. No lexical tone and no pitch accent; stress is not marked melodically.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described: fn. 14 says prior studies make no mention of a hierarchy between stresses of different words or phrases; the authors suspect several degrees of stress but did not study it.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated beyond the long-second-syllable override.
new_statements.domain_note: Rule is stated over 'lexemes' (word level); intonation groups do not interact with stress. Rialland & Robert's own data are Senegalese Wolof (Paris informants, Kajoor/Thiès recordings); the Gambian-Wolof leg of the statement rests on their citation of Njie 1982: 53, which I could not open. The SPA 1979 digest of Sauvageot 1965 (p. 41) adds that stress is 'not distinctive' and that the first syllable is 'generally stressed', with length the main phonetic correlate.
new_statements.identity_note: No opened source describes Gambian Wolof [gamb1252] stress first-hand. The quoted rule is from Rialland & Robert 2001, whose corpus is Senegalese Wolof (Glottolog Wolof/Nuclear Wolof, nucl1347 / wolo1247 — already in the catalog under nucl1347 with this same passage plus Kobès 1869); it reaches Gambian Wolof only through their citation of Njie 1982: 53 (Description syntaxique du wolof de Gambie). The Gambian materials actually opened (Peace Corps 1995 manual, Sosseh 1965) are silent on stress. Ward 1939 (Bathurst informants) is the one first-hand Gambian phonetic description located, paywalled.

sources.note: STRESS field: '"Stress is not distinctive." (p. 41) The first syllable of a word is generally stressed. Stress is realized phonetically as a combination of length, intensity, and pitch, the first being the most prominent factor. (See p. 41-44.)' — digest of Sauvageot 1965 (Dyolof, Senegal); sources listed also include Ward 1939 (Gambia and Senegal) and Manessy & Sauvageot 1963.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Gambian. 'Pronounciation guide' (p. 2) treats only vowel length (long vowels doubled, 'sometimes the only way to distinguish pairs of words') and prenasalised consonants; nothing on stress or accent. 'Stress' appears later only as a grammatical term for the emphatic predicators (laa/nga/dafa). Live URL 404; Internet Archive copy 2017-12-09; text layer font-shifted, decoded copy.
